articles.title: Shannon Lucid’s Record-Setting Mission Aboard Mir

articles.content:
Astronaut Shannon W. Lucid checked on wheat plants aboard Russia’s Mir Space Station on Sept. 23, 1996. Lucid left Mir later that day along with the rest of the STS-79 crew except for John E. Blaha, who was beginning a four-month stay aboard the station. NASA

Shannon Lucid’s Record-Setting Mission Aboard Mir

Three days before returning to Earth, Shannon W. Lucid—who joined NASA in 1978 as one of its first six female astronauts—checked in on wheat growing in the Svet greenhouse aboard the Russian space station Mir. For six months, Lucid lived and worked alongside two Russian cosmonauts conducting life science studies and other experiments in microgravity.

Lucid returned to Earth aboard space shuttle Atlantis on Sept. 26, 1996, completing a 188-day mission—a new record for both a woman and for an American. Lessons from her time on Mir helped NASA prepare for the psychological and cultural challenges of long-duration missions on the International Space Station.

In December 1996, President Bill Clinton awarded Shannon Lucid the Congressional Space Medal of Honor for her achievement. She was the tenth person and the first woman to receive this award.

After her mission on Mir, Lucid continued to serve NASA in key roles on the ground. She worked as a CAPCOM in Mission Control, where she was the primary voice communicating with astronauts in orbit. Later, she served as NASA’s Chief Scientist, helping guide the agency’s science priorities. Lucid retired from NASA in 2012 after a career that spanned more than three decades.

articles.personality_title: Shannon Lucid sets record with 188-day mission aboard Mir space station
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – In 1996, NASA astronaut Shannon Lucid spent time on the Russian space station Mir. She was one of the first women chosen as an astronaut by NASA back in 1978.

**What happened** – Shannon Lucid lived and worked on Mir for 188 days, from March to September 1996. During this time, she joined two Russian cosmonauts to do science experiments in space, including checking on wheat plants growing in a special greenhouse. She returned to Earth on September 26, 1996, aboard the space shuttle Atlantis.

**Impact** – Lucid’s 188-day stay set a new record for the longest time a woman and an American had spent in space. Her work helped NASA learn how to handle the challenges of living in space for a long time, such as dealing with different cultures and staying healthy. This experience was important for future missions on the International Space Station.

**What's next step** – After her mission, Lucid continued to support NASA by helping communicate with astronauts in space and guiding science projects. Her mission helped NASA prepare for even longer space trips in the future.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Shannon Lucid’s record-breaking mission aboard Mir advanced NASA’s ability to explore space for long periods and opened doors for women in space science.

articles.title: NASA’s Hubble Telescope Reaches Milestone, Looks for Elusive Supernova
articles.summary: NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope captured this image of massive galaxy cluster MACS J0417 (left of center) on Sept. 19, 2026. This galaxy cluster acts as a gravitational lens, bending and magnifying light from objects far behind it. Supernova Athena, discovered by NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope in 2025, is predicted to reappear between now and […]
articles.content:
An image from NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope of galaxy cluster MACS J0417 is part of repeated observations to monitor for the reappearance of supernova Athena, which can help astronomers measure the expansion rate of the universe. NASA, ESA, STScI, M. Pascale (UCLA); Image Processing: J. DePasquale (STScI)

NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope captured this image of massive galaxy cluster MACS J0417 (left of center) on Sept. 19, 2026. This galaxy cluster acts as a gravitational lens, bending and magnifying light from objects far behind it. Supernova Athena, discovered by NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope in 2025, is predicted to reappear between now and early March 2027. Measuring the timing of Athena’s reappearances can help researchers map the mass of MACS J0417, which acts as a magnifying, foreground lens for distant objects, and refine our understanding of the expansion rate of the universe.

Hubble also completed its 200,000th orbit around Earth on Sept. 19, marking another new milestone for an observatory that continues to transform our understanding of the universe.

Read more about Hubble and this recent milestone.

Image credit: NASA, ESA, STScI, M. Pascale (UCLA); Image Processing: J. DePasquale (STScI)

articles.personality_title: Hubble Space Telescope marks 200,000 orbits while tracking rare supernova
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – NASA's Hubble Space Telescope has been orbiting Earth since 1990, capturing images and data that help scientists study space. One tool it uses is observing galaxy clusters, which can bend light like a magnifying glass, making distant objects easier to see.

**What happened** – On September 19, 2026, Hubble took a new image of a huge galaxy cluster called MACS J0417. This cluster acts as a gravitational lens, bending light from faraway objects behind it. Scientists are watching for the return of a supernova named Athena, first found by NASA's James Webb Space Telescope in 2025. Athena is expected to appear again between late 2026 and early 2027. At the same time, Hubble reached its 200,000th orbit around Earth, a new milestone for the telescope.

**Impact** – Tracking when supernova Athena reappears helps researchers learn more about the mass of the galaxy cluster MACS J0417. This information improves how we measure the universe’s expansion, which tells us how fast space itself is growing. Hubble’s milestone shows how long this telescope has been helping scientists make important discoveries.

**What's next step** – Scientists will continue watching the galaxy cluster and the supernova’s return. The data from these observations will be used to better understand the universe’s growth and the role of massive galaxy clusters in bending light. Hubble will keep orbiting and sending back valuable information for future space studies.

**One-sentence takeaway** – NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope reached 200,000 orbits while helping track a rare supernova, advancing our knowledge of the universe’s expansion.

articles.personality_title_es: El telescopio espacial Hubble alcanza 200,000 órbitas mientras sigue una supernova rara
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – El telescopio espacial Hubble de la NASA ha estado orbitando la Tierra desde 1990, capturando imágenes y datos que ayudan a los científicos a estudiar el espacio. Utiliza cúmulos de galaxias que funcionan como lentes gravitacionales, doblando la luz para ver objetos muy lejanos.

**Qué pasó** – El 19 de septiembre de 2026, Hubble tomó una nueva imagen de un enorme cúmulo de galaxias llamado MACS J0417. Este cúmulo actúa como una lente gravitacional, doblando la luz de objetos distantes detrás de él. Los científicos esperan que reaparezca una supernova llamada Athena, descubierta en 2025 por el telescopio espacial James Webb de la NASA. Se espera que Athena vuelva a verse entre finales de 2026 y principios de 2027. Ese mismo día, Hubble completó su órbita número 200,000 alrededor de la Tierra, un nuevo récord para el telescopio.

**Impacto** – Seguir la reaparición de la supernova Athena ayuda a los investigadores a entender mejor la masa del cúmulo de galaxias MACS J0417. Esta información mejora las mediciones de la expansión del universo, mostrando qué tan rápido crece el espacio. El hito también demuestra cuánto tiempo ha ayudado Hubble a los científicos a hacer importantes descubrimientos.

**Próximo paso** – Los científicos continuarán observando el cúmulo de galaxias y el regreso de la supernova. Los datos de estas observaciones se usarán para entender mejor el crecimiento del universo y el papel de los grandes cúmulos de galaxias en doblar la luz. Hubble seguirá orbitando y enviando información valiosa para futuros estudios espaciales.

**Conclusión en una frase** – El telescopio espacial Hubble de la NASA alcanzó 200,000 órbitas mientras ayuda a seguir una supernova rara, avanzando en nuestro conocimiento sobre la expansión del universo.
